title: US Nears Deal for Stake in Venezuelan Oil Fields as OPEC+ Loses Market Sway to China
subhead: Washington is closing in on a deal to lock in long-term access to Venezuelan crude — a move that could reshape the Western Hemisphere's oil map — while a Reuters analysis shows OPEC+ has lost its grip on prices six months into the Iran war, with China filling the vacuum.

sections.heading: US Moves to Lock In Venezuelan Oil as Strategic Reserves Sit at 40-Year Low
sections.body:
The Trump administration is working on a deal to secure long-term US access to a group of Venezuelan oilfields, Reuters reports, citing insiders who say an agreement could be signed and made public soon. A list of 17 fields in negotiation includes green fields in the Orinoco Belt and mature areas in Lake Maracaibo, some currently operated by a small Chinese firm whose contract dates to the Maduro era. A 'lease' is under consideration as the legal model, with a possible auction to allocate fields among US producers.

The deal faces real obstacles: Venezuela's current hydrocarbons law does not provide for acreage leases, the constitution reserves core industry activity to the state, and experts cited by Al Jazeera say the arrangement could raise constitutional questions and face legal challenges. The context is stark — the US strategic petroleum reserve is at a 40-year low, per Hindustan Times, and US refineries are already taking in roughly half of Venezuela's oil output, according to an earlier official statement.
sections.whyItMatters: This is Washington converting a military intervention into a permanent supply arrangement — effectively annexing the world's largest proven crude reserves into the US energy base. It also signals a shift in how the US thinks about energy security: not just sanctions and reserves, but direct ownership of foreign production.

sections.heading: OPEC+ Loses Its Grip on Prices as China Fills the Power Vacuum
sections.body:
Six months into the Iran war, OPEC+ is confronting a structural loss of influence, according to a Reuters analysis published Thursday. The alliance accounted for about 40% of global oil production in July, down from more than 48% before the US and Israel launched attacks on Iran in late February. Part of the decline stems from the UAE's decision to leave OPEC in May, but the war created a deeper problem: producers cannot physically move the crude they claim to produce.

Since March, OPEC+'s core group has announced six output increases, but much of that additional production 'has effectively existed only on paper' because the crude cannot reach international buyers through the constrained Strait of Hormuz. The market's central question has shifted from how much OPEC+ wants to produce to how much it can actually export. Meanwhile China has emerged as a counterweight, with its reduced crude imports and market behavior increasingly setting the tone for prices, per the analysis and IBTimes coverage.
sections.whyItMatters: The cartel that spent decades setting the price of oil is now a paper tiger on supply. With the UAE gone and Gulf exporters physically constrained, the marginal price-setter is increasingly China's demand — a quiet but profound transfer of market power away from the producers' alliance.

sections.heading: Hormuz Diplomacy Stalls as Trump Rejects June Ceasefire Terms
sections.body:
Oil prices firmed Thursday after the Wall Street Journal reported that President Trump told mediators he was not interested in returning to the terms of a June ceasefire deal with Iran, dampening hopes that an Iran-Oman revenue-sharing arrangement over the Strait of Hormuz could open the door to a wider deal. Brent traded near $90 for the October contract, while WTI climbed 1.6% to $84 a barrel, per CNBC-TV18.

Gulf states had launched a wave of diplomatic activity — Qatar's prime minister met Iran's lead negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf to discuss conditions for resuming talks with the US. But Tehran maintained that any navigation agreement would not mean an immediate reopening of the chokepoint, and the White House said it was not negotiating with Iran, with Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt telling reporters the naval blockade would stay in place, per Bloomberg.
sections.whyItMatters: The diplomatic window that briefly opened in June has closed. Washington is betting on sanctions and blockade pressure rather than a negotiated reopening of Hormuz, which means the physical constraint on Gulf exports — and the price premium it carries — is likely to persist into the autumn.

sections.heading: Asia's Soft Imports Challenge US Claims of a Hormuz Rebound
sections.body:
Asia, the biggest market for Gulf crude, is set to import 23.12 million barrels per day in August, slightly down from 23.36 million bpd in July, per Kpler data cited by Reuters columnist Clyde Russell. Imports from the Middle East inched up to 11.11 million bpd from 10.76 million bpd — but remain more than 4 million bpd below the 15.82 million bpd average of the three months before the war.

The data undercuts claims by US Energy Secretary Chris Wright, who said in mid-August that Middle East oil exports had rebounded to 15 million bpd and even topped the pre-war average of 20 million bpd on some days. Ship-tracking data shows flows out of Hormuz are, at best, half that figure, per Oilprice.com. The modest August uptick may simply reflect vessels that raced to exit the chokepoint during the brief June-July ceasefire.
sections.whyItMatters: The gap between official US claims of a rebound and the actual shipping data matters because it shapes market expectations. If the rebound is overstated, the market is underpricing the persistence of the Hormuz constraint — and the risk of a sharper price move when reality catches up.

sections.heading: Europe Heads Into Winter With Gas Storage at a Two-Decade Low
sections.body:
Europe is entering winter with gas storage at its lowest level in two decades, as disrupted Middle East LNG flows leave the continent losing the battle with Asia for scarce cargoes, pushing TTF and northwest European LNG prices to their highest levels, per multiple reports. Analysts cited by MSN warn prices could top €100 per megawatt-hour this winter.

The squeeze traces back to the war: Qatar's LNG exports have fallen by 96% over six months of the US-Israeli conflict with Iran, according to The Insider, and Europe risks entering winter with half-empty storage facilities. US LNG producers have shipped record volumes so far in 2026, but Reuters notes rising global gas prices may soon curb demand from cost-sensitive buyers — an endurance test for the US export boom.
sections.whyItMatters: Europe's gas problem is no longer a Russia story — it is now a Middle East story. With Qatari supply collapsed and US cargoes increasingly expensive, the continent faces a winter of high prices and thin storage, a direct energy-security consequence of the Iran war that will test European resolve.

sections.heading: US Widens Economic Warfare on Iran, Targeting China's Trade Network
sections.body:
The US Treasury launched 'Operation Economic Outcast' on Monday, a whole-of-government campaign to isolate Iran, designating nearly 60 entities, individuals and vessels across five sectors including digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping, per the Treasury and Asia Times. Among those named were 16 Hong Kong- and Shenzhen-based firms accused of acting as procurement, logistics or shipping fronts for Iran's trade network, including Sweet Ocean Industrial, RPT Technology, Sky Oil and Gas Asia, and Vienna Shipping.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent framed the campaign in sweeping terms, comparing it to the D-Day offensive and warning that 'any entity that facilitates money laundering on behalf of Iran will be removed from the US dollar system.' The move puts China in a dilemma: Beijing wants the conflict to drain US resources, yet is wary of becoming a target of Washington's economic campaign against those who do business with Tehran, per Asia Times.
sections.whyItMatters: The US is now weaponizing the dollar system against third-country intermediaries, not just Iran itself. China's position as Iran's main buyer of discounted crude makes it the central target — and the escalation risks pulling the world's two largest economies into direct economic confrontation over energy trade.

bottomLine: The day's defining development is Washington's move to convert its Venezuela intervention into a permanent oil-supply arrangement — a direct answer to a strategic reserve at a 40-year low. Beneath that, a Reuters analysis confirms OPEC+ has lost its ability to move prices, with China emerging as the market's new center of gravity. Hormuz diplomacy has stalled after Trump rejected June ceasefire terms, Asia's import data undercuts US claims of a rebound, and Europe faces a two-decade-low gas storage position heading into winter. The through-line: the Iran war has permanently reshuffled who controls the world's energy — away from the Gulf producers' cartel and toward Washington's direct supply deals and Beijing's demand.
sources: Reuters, Al Jazeera, Hindustan Times, IBTimes, Oilprice.com, CNBC-TV18, Bloomberg, Wall Street Journal, Asia Times, US Treasury, The Insider, MSN, Kpler
